title: A design-sweep heatmap is only as informative as its colour scale, its caption and the question its metric answers
summary: A purity heatmap, a separation-resolution sweep and a velocity field in a stepped micro-channel are the three typical outputs of a microfluidic design study. Read the metric definition and the caption's own caveats before reading the colours: these figures state that the 2D model cannot produce the separation it is being asked about.

media.alt: Heatmap with six rows (eel channel widths 100 to 500 micrometres and a serpentine channel) and five columns (flow rate 0.3 to 0.7 millilitres per minute). Every cell is a dark blue-violet with printed values between 0.25 and 0.29 on a colour scale running from 0 to 1. The title says that 2D structurally cannot produce genuine size-based inertial separation, and a footer says placeholder coefficients.

source.caption: Microfluidics outlet-purity heatmap
source.note: The two sweep figures carry their own caveat in the title: the 2D stand-in model cannot represent Dean-vortex-driven separation, and the footer says placeholder coefficients were used. The page therefore teaches the generic reading only and draws no performance claim.

read_the_figure.question: Which design choices (channel width, shape, flow rate) separate particles best, measured by a stated metric, and is the model able to show that at all?
read_the_figure.axes: Heatmap: rows are channel designs, columns are flow rates in mL/min, colour and printed number are outlet purity from 0 to 1 (mean of the majority-class purity of the low and high outlet branches, at a split position of 0.5). Resolution figure: left, separation resolution Rs against flow rate for each channel, with a dotted line at Rs = 1 labelled baseline resolved; right, Rs against channel width at five fixed flow rates. Micromixer figure: x and y are position in micrometres, colour is flow speed |u| in mm/s.
look_at: The colour scale first: 0 to 1 with purity values that are all within about 0.04 of one another means the map shows no design effect.
The title and footer: here they say the 2D model cannot give genuine size-based inertial separation and that coefficients are placeholders. They override any reading of the colours as performance.
The Rs figure: how far the curves sit below the Rs = 1 line. All of them are far below it.
The one design that stands apart (the narrowest, 100 micrometres) and whether it rises with flow rate.
Micromixer field: a parabolic speed profile across each straight leg, a stagnant wall layer, and the speed in each leg staying about the same where the width is constant.
read_the_figure.proves: The heatmap and sweep show that the pipeline of geometry, flow solve, particle tracing and metric extraction runs end to end across a design grid. They do not show that any design separates particles, and the figures say so. The velocity field shows a mass-conserving Stokes solve in a multi-leg channel.
if_wrong: All cells nearly equal and near chance: the physics that drives the separation is missing from the model (here named in the title), or the metric is insensitive.
Rs rising with flow rate for the narrowest channel only: a geometry effect, not a mechanism, until shown otherwise.
A velocity field with speed that is not uniform between equal-width legs: a mass-conservation or boundary-condition error.
A heatmap whose colour range is compressed to the data range: it would exaggerate tiny differences. Here the range is 0 to 1, which is the honest choice.
must_check: The metric is defined, including the number of particle classes and how outlet branches are formed.
The chance level of the metric is marked; the figure does not say it, and the number of classes is not shown.
The model's applicability is stated (here it is, in the title).
Placeholder or substituted coefficients are labelled on the figure (here they are, in the footer).
The same colour scale across a comparison of figures.
as_drawn: Purity values printed in the cells: 0.27 to 0.29 for the 100 micrometre channel and 0.25 to 0.26 for all others, at every flow rate. The colour scale runs 0 to 1.

Separation resolution Rs: for the 100 micrometre channel about 0.09 at 0.3 mL/min rising to about 0.125 at 0.7 mL/min; for the 200 micrometre channel between about 0.004 and 0.02; for wider channels about 0.001 to 0.012. The Rs = 1 baseline-resolved line is far above all data.

Micromixer: channel width is about 20 micrometres, the maximum speed is about 2.8 mm/s on each leg, and the title reports the mass-conservation residual, which is partly hidden by the colour bar and ends in 43e-11.

terms.meaning: The fraction of particles in an outlet that belong to the majority class. It is 1 for a perfectly sorted outlet and falls to the class share for a random mix.
A chromatography-style measure of how well two peaks are separated: the distance between their means divided by their average width.
Flow at very low Reynolds number in which inertia is negligible and the equations are linear.
Migration of particles across streamlines to preferred positions in a channel, caused by finite-Reynolds-number lift forces, which depends on the cross-section being resolved in three dimensions.
Secondary cross-stream circulation set up in curved channels.
How far the discrete velocity field is from satisfying that the net flux through any closed region is zero; a measure of solver correctness.

remember: A heatmap of a metric that barely varies is a null result: say so and do not read structure into it.
A metric needs a chance level. Without it, 0.25 cannot be interpreted.
In Stokes flow the shape of the velocity profile does not depend on the speed, only its scale.
Mean speed in a channel of constant depth is inversely proportional to its width for fixed flow rate.
A model that cannot represent the mechanism cannot rank designs by that mechanism.

understand.title: Why the caption outranks the colours
understand.text: A parameter sweep is a machine for producing a grid of numbers, so it will produce a grid of numbers whether or not the model contains the physics. Here the title states that the model lacks a resolved third dimension and therefore the secondary flows that drive size-based separation. The grid is then a check of the pipeline, not a result about devices.

understand.title: What the resolution sweep does show
understand.text: Within the stand-in model, the narrowest channel gives a measurable, flow-rate-dependent Rs of about 0.1 while wider channels sit near zero. That is a statement about the stand-in, not about devices. The dotted Rs = 1 line makes the gap to a usable separation obvious.

understand.title: The micromixer field as a correctness view
understand.text: A field of |u| in a stepped channel is a standard sanity picture. Look for no-slip at the walls, a parabolic profile across each leg, similar peak speed in legs of equal width, and a small mass residual. Those are checks on the flow solve that the particle study depends on.

steps.title: Purity of an outlet
steps.note: N_k is the number of particles of class k reaching the outlet. For K equal classes in a perfectly mixed outlet this is 1/K, which is the chance level.

steps.title: Separation resolution
steps.note: Two distributions separated by their mean difference divided by their mean width. The figure's own normalisation is not stated; the dotted line at 1 is its baseline-resolved level.

steps.title: Reynolds number of a micro-channel
steps.note: With speed a few mm/s and width tens of micrometres in water, Re is of order 0.1 or less: inertia is weak, and flow is of Stokes type.

steps.title: Parabolic profile in a plane channel
steps.note: The shape across each straight leg of the micromixer figure, for channel half-width H. Peak speed is one and a half times the mean speed.

steps.title: Mass conservation sets speed against width
steps.note: For constant depth d, a leg of half the width has twice the mean speed. Equal-width legs have equal speed, as in the figure.

worked.title: Reynolds number of the micromixer figure
worked.problem: The peak speed is about 2.8 mm/s and the channel width about 20 micrometres. For water (kinematic viscosity 1e-6 square metres per second) estimate the Reynolds number based on the mean speed and the width.
worked.answer: About 0.04: deep in the Stokes regime. The water viscosity is an assumption; the figure does not state the fluid.

analyze.q: All purity cells are between 0.25 and 0.29. List two reasons the metric might be flat and the run that would separate them.
analyze.hint: Missing physics versus an insensitive metric; a run with a known-separating test case.

analyze.q: Why does the 100 micrometre channel stand out in both the heatmap and the Rs plot, and would you trust that as a design recommendation?
analyze.hint: Geometry versus mechanism, and the title's caveat.

analyze.q: What is the expected purity if the outlet were a random mix of K equal classes, and what does that make of 0.25?
analyze.hint: 1/K; the number of classes is not shown.

evaluate.q: Is it acceptable to publish these figures? What must accompany them?
evaluate.hint: Their own caveat, a definition of the metric and a statement of what they do not show.

evaluate.q: What evidence would convert this pipeline demonstration into a design result?
evaluate.hint: A model with the resolved mechanism, validated against a measured separation.

create: Redraw the heatmap with the chance level marked on the colour bar and the caveat as a banner across the figure.
Design a validation case for the particle tracer: a configuration with a known, published equilibrium position, and the plot that would show agreement.

checks.q: Why can a 2D model not show size-based inertial separation in a curved channel?
checks.hint: The figure's title gives the reason.
checks.answer: The secondary (Dean) flow that moves particles across the channel needs a resolved third dimension; a 2D model has no such flow.

checks.q: A leg of constant depth is narrowed from 20 to 10 micrometres at fixed flow rate. How does the mean speed change?
checks.hint: Mean speed times width is constant.

checks.q: Purity is 0.25 everywhere. Which hypothesis is more consistent: good separation in all designs or none?
checks.answer: None. Equal values at what would be the chance level of a few equal classes say the outlets are essentially unsorted.

checks.q: Rs reaches 0.125 for the narrowest channel. Is the device resolved?
checks.answer: No. It is about an eighth of the baseline-resolved level of 1.

checks.q: How would you add a chance-level reference to the heatmap?
checks.hint: Divide purity by its chance value, or draw a contour.
checks.answer: Plot purity minus 1/K, or draw a contour on the colour bar at 1/K, so that cells at chance are visibly neutral.
